*Theory and Research Note No. 3.4, November 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The Egypt results in Appendix B are the author's illustrative calculations on public data; they are not official estimates of any institution.*

# Executive summary {.unnumbered}

**This note reviews what is known about the energy transition as a macroeconomic event.** It states 32 stylized facts in five groups, sets the literature against each, and draws out what they mean for macroeconomic indicators, for carbon pricing and for development finance. It is a review and not a model. The one modelling exercise, for Egypt, is in Appendix B. The note leads in to further work on a global green deal.

**The transition swaps a fuel bill for a capital bill.** A system that runs on fuel is paid for every day, at prices set abroad. An electric system is paid for when it is built, and its cost is then fixed by the interest rate and the currency of its finance. On the International Energy Agency's net zero path, capital rises from under 60 percent to about 80 percent of the cost of supplying electricity. For a fuel importer, energy moves from the current account to the balance sheet, and the cost of capital becomes the price of energy.

**Investment responds to the relative price that is expected to last.** Energy demand responds little to prices in the short run (an elasticity of about −0.2) and three times as much in the long run, because the response is embodied in machines. Buyers expect today's fuel price to last, and they respond more to a tax change than to an equal change in the market price. Policy uncertainty acts as a tax on investment that cannot be undone, and a carbon price that a later government can reverse is discounted by investors. Expectations must hold at two levels at once: that policy will last, and that the grid, the chargers and the clean power will be there.

**Price and deployment have opposite returns.** Each further cut bought by a price needs a higher price. On a standard demand curve, cutting road fuel use by 10 percent needs about \$80 a tonne of carbon dioxide, and cutting it by 30 percent needs about \$350. Each doubling of deployment makes the next plant cheaper: installed cost has fallen by 34 percent per doubling for solar and 25 percent for onshore wind. The falling cost benefits every country, so each country alone deploys too little.

**The first-best carbon price is a benchmark, and the pragmatic price is one part of a package.** Theory gives one price on all emissions, equal to the damage they do. Estimates of that damage run from \$31 to \$185 a tonne, and the prices consistent with the Paris goals are \$50 to \$100 by 2030. The average price in force is about \$21, on 29 percent of emissions. The second-best literature finds that a price alone is costly where knowledge spills over, capital is long-lived, capital markets fail, governments cannot commit and voters resist. It does not find that the price should be dropped: a price is the best single instrument, and a price set too low costs more than one set too high. @sec-pricing gives seven pragmatic rules. Remove fuel subsidies first. Price operations where the response is quick. Use feebates and standards on new equipment where it is slow. Write the price into contracts. Lower the cost of capital alongside. Announce the sequence. Credit equivalent policies under international price floors.

**In developing countries finance is the binding constraint.** Capital for solar power costs well over twice as much there as in advanced economies. Public entities finance about half of clean energy investment, and state companies own most of the power sector. The scarce asset is the standing of lenders who are paid first: development banks' sovereign loans default at 0.77 percent a year and recover 95 percent. That standing holds only while such lending is limited, and a guarantee is a contingent liability for the country that receives it. Three simple products the World Bank could offer follow from the facts: a payment guarantee on the power contract, a refinancing guarantee for plants and grids once they run, and a guarantee line that grows as reforms are kept. A buffer fund of donor capital stands behind them.

**The macroeconomic profile is investment first and savings later.** The literature puts the extra investment at about 2 percent of GDP a year in advanced economies and much more in developing ones. Estimates of the growth effect run from −0.25 to +0.4 percentage points a year. They differ on whether the transition is led by prices, which is a supply shock, or by financed investment, which adds demand first and supply later. Budgets lose fuel tax revenue and gain contingent liabilities. About half of the capital spending is imported equipment, so the external balance worsens before it improves. @tbl-indicators gives ten indicators that track the change.

**Egypt shows the orders of magnitude.** Egypt has been a net importer of gas since 2024. In the author's illustrative calculations, a rapid transition needs extra investment of 5.3 percent of GDP a year over 2026–35. By 2035 it costs a net 0.5 percent of GDP a year at a local cost of capital of 8.2 percent in real terms, and it saves 0.9 percent of GDP at a de-risked 3.9 percent. Power and transport pay for themselves at either rate, buildings only when de-risked, and industry at neither. The external balance is worse by 1.7 percent of GDP at the start and better from 2032 to 2034. Waiting five years costs \$6 billion to \$32 billion in present value and burns 217 billion cubic meters more gas. The path adds 7.5 gigawatts of wind and solar a year, against a record of 1.5, so much of the engineering and the finance must come from outside consortia.

**Several things are not established.** The size of the growth effect is disputed. The evidence on currency swaps between developing countries and on pension funds as buyers of clean assets is thin. The import share of one-half is an assumption. Expectations cannot be measured directly, only through proxies.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

**The macroeconomics of climate policy has mostly been written as the macroeconomics of a tax.** A carbon price raises the cost of energy, and models trace the effect on output, inflation and revenue. The energy transition under way is a different event. It replaces machines that burn fuel with machines that run on electricity, and power stations that buy fuel with plants that have none to buy. Its macroeconomics is that of a large investment program whose cost depends on finance and whose pace depends on expectations.

**This note asks what the stylized facts of that transition imply for macroeconomic policy.** It takes 32 facts, most of them familiar to energy specialists and few of them joined up in macroeconomic work, and reviews the literature behind each. @sec-facts lists them. @sec-system reviews the physical facts and their theory. @sec-expect reviews prices, expectations and investment under uncertainty. @sec-pricing draws the implications for carbon pricing, first best and second best. @sec-finance turns to contracts and finance, and @sec-macro to the macroeconomic profile and its indicators. @sec-deal sets out the implications and the link to a global green deal.

**The evidence standard is stated so that the reader can discount it.** A source is cited for a number only where its text or abstract was read for this note; the record of what was read is kept with the note. Where a fact rests on thin evidence, the text says so. The estimates for Egypt in Appendix B are the author's illustrative calculations with an open model on public data. They show orders of magnitude and are not official estimates of any institution.

**Three things are new.** The first is the joint reading: the facts are individually known, and their macroeconomic meaning comes from taking them together. The second is the treatment of expectations and of the cost of capital as parts of carbon pricing policy and not as separate subjects. The third is a set of indicators for an economy that is moving from a fuel bill to a capital bill.

# Thirty-two facts in five groups {#sec-facts}

**The facts fall into five groups, and each group changes a different part of macroeconomic policy.** @tbl-groups states the groups. Appendix A gives each fact with its evidence and a verdict: 19 are supported outright, 11 are supported with a qualification, and two rest on theory or on thin evidence.

| Group | The facts in one sentence | What changes for macroeconomic policy |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| A. Energy becomes capital (facts 1–7) | The transition electrifies a system that ran on fuel; clean power is cheap to build, has no fuel, and needs grids and storage | Energy moves from the current account to the balance sheet; the cost of capital becomes the price of energy |
| B. Prices, expectations and investment (8–16) | Carbon prices change operations quickly and are often reversed; investment follows the price that is expected to last; price has diminishing and deployment increasing returns | Credibility becomes a macroeconomic variable; the carbon price is one part of a package |
| C. Contracts, finance and the state (17–23) | Long assets need long contracts with public buyers; capital is dear and budgets are full; development banks are paid first | The constraint is the sovereign balance sheet; guarantees replace subsidies as the fiscal question |
| D. The macroeconomic profile (24–29) | Spending is several percent of GDP, comes first, and is about half imported; fuel savings and lost fuel taxes come later | A J-curve in the external and fiscal accounts that long finance must bridge |
| E. Time and capacity (30–32) | Grids take longest; waiting has a cost that a high discount rate hides; engineering and finance must largely come from outside | Plan the slowest asset first; tender at program scale |

: Five groups of stylized facts and what each changes for macroeconomic policy. The 32 facts and their evidence are in Appendix A. {#tbl-groups}

# Energy becomes capital {#sec-system}

**The first group of facts is physical, and the literature on it is settled.** Electricity is 21 percent of final energy use today. It reaches 50 to 55 percent by 2050 on net zero paths and 31 percent on stated policies [@IEA2021; @IEA2025WEO]. Electric cars are two to four times as efficient as combustion cars, and heat pumps three to five times as efficient as boilers [@IEA2025WEO]. Behavior change and the more efficient use of materials supply about 8 percent of the emission cuts in the International Energy Agency's (IEA) net zero pathway; the rest is equipment that someone must buy [@IEA2021]. Emissions fall because machines are replaced.

**Theory explains why the response to energy prices runs through the capital stock.** Energy use is embodied in machines. In models where energy intensity is fixed when capital is installed, capital and energy are complements in the short run and substitutes in the long run, as the stock turns over [@AtkesonKehoe1999]. The same holds for technology: aggregate data show very little short-run substitution between energy and other inputs, and the long-run response to costly energy comes through technical change directed at saving it [@HasslerKrusellOlovsson2021]. Fact 3 is the empirical face of that theory.

**Clean power is cheap to build and priced by its finance.** In 2024, 91 percent of new renewable capacity produced power more cheaply than the cheapest new fossil plant; onshore wind averaged 3.4 US cents a kilowatt-hour and solar 4.3 [@IRENA2025]. The share of capital in the cost of supplying electricity rises from under 60 percent to about 80 percent on the IEA's net zero path [@IEA2021]. A solar plant that costs \$800 a kilowatt and lasts 25 years sells power 80 percent dearer when its capital costs 12 percent than when it costs 4 (author's calculation, on the stylized plant of @CFPB31). Onshore wind costs the same per kilowatt-hour in Africa as in Europe, and most of the African cost is financing [@IRENA2025]. If discount rates doubled, the cost of gas-fired power would hardly change and that of offshore wind could rise by nearly 45 percent [@Schnabel2023].

**The second half of the transition is dearer and slower than the first.** Wind and solar have no fuel, so they run first when the grid can take them. Where grids lag, 5 to 15 percent of their output is thrown away, as in Chile, and China curtailed about 9 percent in early 2026 [@IEA2024Renewables; @Reuters2026Curtailment]. Batteries have fallen 93 percent in cost since 2010 [@IRENA2025]. Even so, storing half of a solar plant's output adds about three-quarters to its cost, and solar that supplies power in every hour costs two to two-and-a-half times as much as plain solar [@Ember2025Storage; @Ember2025Solar24]. Grids take 5 to 15 years to plan, permit and build, against 1 to 5 for the plants they connect, and grid investment has fallen to under \$0.40 for each dollar spent on generation, from \$0.60 in 2016 [@IEA2023Grids; @IEA2025WEI].

**A grid is worth what it lets cheap power do, and the literature measures that in three ways.** The first is system cost. Europe's network operators estimate that each euro invested in networks saves over two in system costs [@ENTSOE2025], and in a model of a fully renewable United States, coordinated transmission cuts the cost of electricity by 46 percent [@BrownBotterud2021]. The second is the cost of delay: in the IEA's delay case, late grids add 58 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2050 [@IEA2023Grids]. The third treats a line built ahead of need as an option, whose value rises with uncertainty about where and when generation will come; planning that ignores the uncertainty has a measurable cost [@vanderWeijdeHobbs2012]. For Egypt the second measure gives \$1.8 billion of imported gas burned for each year that one year's additions of wind and solar wait for a connection (Appendix B).

**For macroeconomic policy, these facts move energy from the current account to the balance sheet.** A fuel importer pays for energy every year at a price set abroad. Net fossil fuel imports cost the world 1.8 percent of GDP in 2022, and one person in four lives in a country that spends at least 5 percent of GDP on them [@Ember2025Security]. A clean system pays once, by borrowing, and its costs are then fixed in the currency and at the interest rate of the loan. Fuel-price shocks fade from inflation and the terms of trade. Interest-rate, refinancing and exchange-rate risks take their place. Four indicators follow: the share of electricity in final energy, the share of capital in the cost of power, the cost of capital for a power project, and the ratio of grid investment to generation investment.

# Prices, expectations and investment under uncertainty {#sec-expect}

**Prices work on two margins, and the literature finds them very different in size.** The first is operation. Britain's carbon price floor cut power sector emissions by 20 to 26 percent a year over 2013–17, by changing which plants ran and closing the dirtiest [@Leroutier2022]. Across 21 carbon pricing schemes, emissions fell by 5 to 21 percent [@Dobbeling2024]. The second margin is investment. One review finds fuel switching in existing plants and no effect worth the name on zero-carbon investment [@Lilliestam2021]; a reply finds a small, positive effect on low-carbon innovation [@vandenBergh2021]. The demand side shows the same split. A meta-analysis puts the price elasticity of energy demand at −0.22 in the short run and −0.65 in the long run [@Labandeira2017].

**The long-run response is a response to expectations.** A machine bought today is run for years, so what matters is the relative price of fuel and electricity over its life. Consumers' forecasts of future gasoline prices are, on average, today's price [@AndersonKelloggSallee2013], and car buyers value future fuel costs at about the interest rates at which they borrow [@BusseKnittelZettelmeyer2013]. Consumers respond more to a change in the fuel tax than to an equal change in the price: about three times as much in the United States and in Sweden [@LiLinnMuehlegger2014; @Andersson2019], and more also in British Columbia [@RiversSchaufele2015]. A tax is visible and is expected to stay, where a market price may fall back; that reading is the author's and fits the forecasting evidence. Innovation follows expected prices too. Energy patents rise with energy prices [@Popp2002], and car makers facing 10 percent higher fuel prices file about 10 percent more clean patents, with strong dependence on their own past direction [@Aghion2016].

**Uncertainty turns an expected return into a reason to wait.** Where an investment cannot be undone and can be postponed, the chance to wait for information has a value, and uncertainty raises it [@Bernanke1983; @Pindyck1991; @DixitPindyck1994]. Pindyck draws the policy lesson: where the aim is to stimulate investment, stability and credibility may matter more than tax incentives or interest rates [@Pindyck1991]. In developing countries even moderate doubt about whether a reform will last acts as a heavy tax on investment [@Rodrik1991], and measured policy uncertainty goes with lower investment in the sectors most exposed to policy [@BakerBloomDavis2016]. The climate literature separates two kinds of uncertainty. Volatility in the carbon price can bring investment forward; doubt about whether the government will keep the policy postpones it [@Fuss2008]. Across 12 countries, climate policy uncertainty goes with lower investment in capital-intensive and pollution-intensive firms [@Berestycki2022]. It goes with less venture funding for clean technology [@Noailly2022], and one legal challenge in the United States raised the cost of meeting a pollution rule by \$124 million by delaying efficient investment [@Dorsey2019].

**A government cannot easily promise a future carbon price.** The optimal plan announced today is not the plan a later government will want to carry out [@KydlandPrescott1977]. Once the clean plant is built, the temptation is to lower the price, and investors know it [@HelmHepburnMash2003; @Brunner2012]. Where owners of fossil assets can lobby, the only announcements that are believed are a price of zero and a price high enough to stop fossil investment at once [@Kalkuhl2020]. The record fits. In 2026 the European Union postponed its carbon market for buildings and road fuel to 2028 and proposed to slow the cap of its main market after ten member states called the system an existential risk [@ICAP2026; @CarbonBrief2026]. Fuel price rises brought riots in 41 countries in 2005–18 [@McCulloch2022], and most French voters would reject a carbon tax even with its revenue returned to them [@DouenneFabre2022]. Support depends on whether people think a policy works and whom they think it hurts [@Dechezlepretre2025]. Against this, coverage keeps growing: direct carbon prices now cover 29 percent of world emissions and raised \$107 billion in 2025 [@WorldBank2026Carbon].

**Expectations must hold at two levels at once.** The first level is policy: the price, the tariff or the standard must be expected to last. The second is the system. An electric car pays only if chargers and cheap power arrive; a wind farm pays only if the line is built; a heat pump pays only if electricity is priced fairly against gas. Each of these is decided by a different body, and each decision can be reversed. Technologies with increasing returns can lock in a path that is not the efficient one and that ordinary taxes do not easily change [@Arthur1989]. A recent model with these frictions finds that the transition is limited less by the cost of stranding old capital than by the rate at which clean capital can expand [@Campiglio2026]. This is why the transition is a coordination problem as well as a pricing problem.

**Two irreversibilities pull in opposite directions, and the literature finds that waiting usually costs more.** Sunk capital argues for waiting until policy and technology are clearer. Emissions that stay in the atmosphere argue for acting now [@ArrowFisher1974; @Kolstad1996; @Pindyck2000]. Falling technology costs add a third argument, for waiting until equipment is cheaper. Most results come down against delay. Delay lengthens the transition and has large welfare costs when innovation responds to policy [@Acemoglu2012; @Acemoglu2016]. Because abatement capital is long-lived, investment should start high even where the optimal price starts low [@VogtSchilb2018], and using the cheapest options first can lock in a path that makes later targets too costly [@VogtSchilbHallegatte2014]. A carbon tax set too low because of optimism costs far more than one set too high because of pessimism [@HasslerKrusellOlovsson2021b]. For a fuel importer the argument from falling costs is weak: a plant bought next year is a few percent cheaper, and the fuel burned in the meantime costs more than that.

**Price and deployment have opposite returns to scale.** @fig-returns shows both. Diminishing returns to price means that each equal step in the price cuts less than the one before, so the price needed for a further cut rises. With a long-run elasticity of −0.5, cutting road fuel use by 10 percent needs a carbon price of about \$80 a tonne, 20 percent needs \$190 and 30 percent needs \$350. This is an illustration with one elasticity; the evidence that carbon prices cut road fuel and heating emissions by 1 to 2 percent for each \$10 a tonne is consistent with it [@StrettonWP55]. Increasing returns to deployment means that each doubling of installed capacity makes the next unit cheaper. Installed cost has fallen by 34 percent per doubling for solar and 25 percent for onshore wind [@IRENA2025], and the evidence points to causation running mainly from deployment at scale to lower cost [@Grubb2021]. Measures that look dear on today's costs can therefore be cheap once the fall in cost they cause is counted [@GillinghamStock2018]. Support for solar beyond the carbon price is justified in most cases, and for onshore wind in fewer [@Newbery2018]. The gain from lower costs goes to every later buyer in every country. A fast transition saves the world \$5 trillion to \$12 trillion, depending on the discount rate [@Way2022]; no single country captures that, and so each deploys too little.

![Returns to a carbon price and returns to deployment. Left: the carbon price needed to cut road fuel use through the price alone, for a long-run price elasticity of −0.5 and a fuel cost of \$0.80 a liter (illustration). Right: installed cost against doublings of cumulative capacity at the rates estimated for 2010–24, world. Sources: author's calculations; @IRENA2025.](2.Source/figures/fig1-returns.png){#fig-returns width=92%}

**Expectations cannot be observed, but six proxies can.** They are: the share of new clean capacity built under contracts of 15 years or more; the gap between the cost of capital of a power project and the government's own borrowing cost; the number of scheduled price or tariff steps that were postponed or reversed in the last ten years; a news-based index of climate policy uncertainty [@Berestycki2022; @Noailly2022]; the number of years over which the carbon price is set in law or in contracts; and the electric share of new vehicle and equipment sales, which shows what buyers believe. None of them measures the expected long-run relative price itself. Together they show whether policy is believed.

# Optimal and pragmatic second-best carbon pricing {#sec-pricing}

**The first-best benchmark is one price on all emissions, equal to the damage they do.** In a general-equilibrium model the optimal tax is proportional to GDP and depends only on discounting, the damage from warming and how long carbon stays in the atmosphere [@Golosov2014]. Estimates of the damage differ by a factor of six: \$31 a tonne of carbon dioxide in one standard model and \$185 in a recent study that uses a 2 percent discount rate [@Nordhaus2017; @Rennert2022]. A second approach takes the temperature goal as given and asks what price delivers it. The answers are at least \$40 to \$80 by 2020 and \$50 to \$100 by 2030 for the Paris goals, "provided a supportive policy environment is in place" [@HLCCP2017], and \$77 to \$124 in 2030 for a United States path to net zero [@Kaufman2020]. In a model where warming follows cumulative emissions, the optimal price starts relatively high and grows relatively fast [@DietzVenmans2019]. Practice is far from the benchmark. The average price in force is about \$21 a tonne on 29 percent of emissions [@WorldBank2026Carbon], and governments still spend \$725 billion a year on explicit fossil fuel subsidies, which are a negative carbon price [@Black2025FFS].

**Each condition behind the benchmark fails in a way that the stylized facts describe.** One price is optimal only if the climate externality is the one failure, if capital markets work, if the government can commit, and if other prices are right [@LipseyLancaster1956]. @tbl-secondbest sets the failures against the facts and against what the literature recommends for each.

| Where the benchmark fails | Facts | What the literature finds | Instrument that answers it |
|:------------------|:--------|:---------------------------------------|:--------------------|
| Knowledge and learning spill over | 12 | The best policy pairs a carbon tax with support for clean technology; relying on the tax alone has significant welfare costs [@Acemoglu2012; @Acemoglu2016; @FischerNewell2008] | Support for deployment and research |
| Abatement is long-lived capital | 3, 30 | Investment should start high even if the price starts low, and its cost per tonne should differ across sectors [@VogtSchilb2018] | Sector programs; standards on new equipment |
| Capital markets fail | 18 | At a carbon price of \$50, a 3 percent cost of capital gives about 40 percent renewable power and a 15 percent cost almost none [@HirthSteckel2016] | Guarantees that lower the cost of capital |
| Governments cannot commit | 9, 14 | An announced tax is discounted; contracts that fix the carbon price cut the cost of capital [@Kalkuhl2020; @RichsteinNeuhoff2022] | Price floors; contracts on the carbon price |
| Voters and incumbents resist | 10 | Standards and feebates on new investment cost more in total and avoid stranded assets [@Jenkins2014; @Rozenberg2020] | Feebates; rebates by output; sequencing |
| Other prices are wrong | 15, 19 | Fuel subsidies make the price negative; retail mark-ups weaken or reverse the case for pricing in power [@Black2025FFS; @BorensteinKellogg2023] | Subsidy and tariff reform first |
| Fuel is traded | 16 | Demand cuts lower world prices and others burn more [@Sinn2008]; in industry, leakage has not been found after the fact [@IPCC2022Ch13] | Supply-side and international agreements [@Harstad2012] |

: Where the first-best carbon price fails, which stylized facts describe the failure, and the instrument the literature sets against it. Fact numbers refer to Appendix A. {#tbl-secondbest}

**Second-best theory does not say that the price should be dropped; it says that the price cannot work alone.** Where several failures are present and only some can be corrected, using several instruments can be optimal, though not every mix in use is justified [@BennearStavins2007; @GoulderParry2008]. In a model of United States electricity the emissions price is the best single instrument, and a portfolio aimed at emissions, learning and research reaches the same cut at a much lower cost [@FischerNewell2008]. Hepburn, Stern and Stiglitz call carbon pricing essential and give four reasons why it will not be enough alone [@HepburnSternStiglitz2020]; others reach the same view by different routes [@Stiglitz2019; @SternStiglitz2021; @BlanchardGollierTirole2023; @IMF2023FM]. The other instruments have costs of their own. Standards and feebates on new investment cost more in total than a tax [@Rozenberg2020]. Renewable subsidies give higher welfare than a tax when policy is mild, and lower when targets are strict [@Baldwin2020]. Leaders who built support with green industrial policy before they priced carbon also created rents and lock-in [@Meckling2017; @Pahle2018].

**Seven pragmatic rules follow for a finance ministry.** They take the price as far as it will go and use other instruments for what it cannot do.

1. *Count the whole price, and remove negative prices first.* The effective carbon price on a fuel is its taxes and permits less its subsidies. Egypt brought retail fuel prices to cost recovery in December 2025 [@IMF2026Egypt7].
2. *Price operations where the capital already exists.* Power dispatch and industrial fuel choice respond within months (fact 8).
3. *Where the response is slow and resistance is high, put the price on new equipment.* A feebate charges dirty equipment and rewards clean, and a rebate by output keeps the price at the margin in traded industry without the full bill [@CFPB12; @Fischer2001; @Bohringer2023].
4. *Turn the price into a contract.* A floor makes the price harder to reverse [@WoodJotzo2011]. A contract that pays the difference between an agreed carbon price and the market price cut the break-even price of a clean steel plant from about 93 euros to 66, and its cost of capital from 16.3 percent to 5.9 [@RichsteinNeuhoff2022].
5. *Lower the cost of capital alongside.* In Egypt, de-risking clean power is worth as much to the investor as a carbon price of about \$45 a tonne on the gas it displaces (Appendix B). It does so without raising anyone's energy bill; its cost is a contingent liability (@sec-finance).
6. *Announce the sequence.* Long-lived assets come first, and the price rises on a path set in law [@VogtSchilb2018; @Fay2015; @Hallegatte2024].
7. *Agree floors by income level, and credit equivalent policies.* IMF staff have proposed a floor among large emitters of \$25, \$50 and \$75 a tonne by income group, with credit for policies that cut emissions by as much [@ParryBlackRoaf2021]. Egypt is among the six largest exporters of the goods covered by the European Union's border carbon charge [@IMF2026Egypt56], so a domestic price that the charge recognizes keeps revenue at home [@CFPB14; @CFPB62].

# Contracts, finance and the sovereign balance sheet {#sec-finance}

**Long assets are built against long contracts, and a contract is only as good as the buyer.** Policy schemes, mostly auctions for long-term contracts, are expected to drive 84 percent of utility-scale renewable growth to 2030; plants that sell at market prices are under 1 percent [@IEA2024Renewables]. The industrial economics literature explains why: a long contract signed before the investment lowers investors' risk premia and eases credit, and contracts that fix the price are the most effective hedge and the cheapest to finance [@Fabra2021; @NeuhoffMayRichstein2022]. Power markets are moving toward a hybrid, with competition for long contracts and short-term markets for dispatch [@Joskow2022]. The buyer is usually the state. Public entities finance about half of clean energy investment in emerging and developing economies, and state-owned companies hold nearly two-thirds of the world's generating capacity [@IEAIFC2023; @Benoit2022]. State companies face soft budget constraints, which weaken their response to prices and return their losses to the budget [@Kornai1986].

**The literature agrees on the size of the cost-of-capital gap and on what it does.** Capital for solar costs well over twice as much in emerging and developing economies as in advanced ones, and financing is half or more of the cost of their power [@IEA2024]. In models, region-specific capital costs cut green electricity in Africa by 35 percent on a cost-optimal 2°C path [@Ameli2021]. Financing conditions matter in rich countries too: in Germany, lower interest rates and lenders' experience account for 5 percent of the fall in the cost of solar power and 24 percent of the fall for wind [@EgliSteffenSchmidt2018]. The budget cannot absorb the gap. Countries that are home to 3.7 billion people spend more on interest than on health or education [@UNCTAD2026].

**The scarce asset is the standing of lenders who are paid first.** On sovereign lending by development banks, defaults averaged 0.77 percent a year and recoveries 95.1 percent over 1984–2024 [@GEMs2025]. The World Bank's main lending arm, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), reports no loss of contractual principal or interest on any past case, with two cases outstanding [@IBRD2024Defaults]. Sovereigns do in fact pay multilateral lenders first [@Schlegl2019]. Theory treats that standing as an equilibrium. A preferred lender is always repaid while it lends limited amounts and does not price for risk, and it loses the status if it lends too much [@CordellaPowell2021]. Rating agencies treat it as conditional in the same way [@SP2026IBRD].

**De-risking is cheap and not free, and its critics have a point.** A guarantee of a state utility's payments rests on the record of public borrowers that are not sovereigns: defaults of 2.61 percent a year and recoveries of 85.8 percent, an expected loss of about 0.4 percent a year [@GEMs2025]. A guarantee that takes 1.4 points off the cost of capital, as in the stylized case of an earlier paper [@CFPB31], then saves about four dollars of interest for each dollar of expected loss. Three limits apply. The guarantee is a contingent liability of the host and belongs on its books. The critical literature adds that de-risking moves investors' risks to the balance sheet of the state and narrows its later choices [@Gabor2021]. And a development bank holds capital against a guarantee as against a loan, so guarantees alone do not stretch its balance sheet [@HumphreyPrizzon2014]. Outside capital behind the guarantee does: \$1 of donor guarantees lets the Asian Development Bank lend up to \$5 more [@ADB2023IFCAP]. India's solar intermediary shows the gain and the limit. It stands between generators and state distributors, is rated AAA, and has contracted 66 gigawatts at an average of Rs 2.74 a unit; about 42 gigawatts more were awarded with no distributor signing [@ICRA2026; @JMK2025]. A guarantee makes the generator whole. It does not make the utility solvent.

**Currency and savings shape what finance can do, and here the evidence is thin.** Revenues are in local currency, and equipment is priced in its supplier's. Local money is dear where inflation is high: Egypt's one-year Treasury bills pay 26 percent [@Enterprise2026CBE]. Money in the supplier's currency can be cheap with a guarantee. Egypt's yen bonds of June 2026, partly guaranteed by the African Development Bank, pay 2.9 to 3.5 percent, and its central bank's swap line with China was raised to 30 billion yuan [@Enterprise2026Samurai; @Xinhua2026Swap]. Two cautions come from the literature. Market hedges of developing-country currencies have cost about 2.2 points a year more than the losses they covered [@Persaud2023], and China's rescue lending through swap lines is opaque and carries relatively high interest rates [@Horn2023]. No project financed through a swap between two developing countries' currencies was found. On savings there is theory only. An aging workforce accumulates assets, a second demographic dividend that depends on policy [@LeeMason2006]. Funded pensions would be natural holders of operating plants in local currency, but no data on their size was found for this note.

**Three simple products follow, each from an earlier paper in this series.** @tbl-products states each in a sentence. The World Bank Group already guarantees loans and payments, through one platform since 2024, and aims to issue \$20 billion of guarantees a year by 2030 [@WorldBank2024Guarantee]. The proposals differ in three ways. One standard contract and one guaranteed buyer serve a whole program of plants. A second stage refinances assets once they run. And the size of a country's guarantee line is tied to reforms kept, among them the tariff and carbon-price steps of @sec-pricing. The first product guarantees the contract and not the debt, because the buyer is the risk: in a stylized case it removes the whole risk premium, where a guarantee on project debt removes under a third of it [@CFPB31]. The second cuts the price of solar power by about a fifth in a stylized case [@CFPB32]. For the third, \$3.3 billion of guarantee capacity is worth \$772 million to a government [@CFPB43; @CFPB41]. The scale is the difficulty. Egypt's illustrative program alone needs \$13.5 billion of power investment a year (Appendix B). Because a guarantee uses capital as a loan does, the products add to lending only with a buffer fund of donor capital behind them [@CFPB42].

| Product | What the Bank would do, in one sentence | Facts it answers | Paper |
|:----------------|:--------------------------------------------|:---------------------|:---------|
| 1. Payment guarantee | Guarantee that the public buyer of the power pays generators on time, under one standard contract for a whole program | The buyer is the risk (17, 19, 21) | 3.1 |
| 2. Refinancing guarantee | Guarantee part of a bond that refinances plants and grids once they run, some of it in local currency | Construction finance is dear; grids have no power contract (6, 18, 22) | 3.2 |
| 3. Reform-linked guarantee line | Enlarge a country's guarantee line as it keeps agreed reforms | Policy can be reversed (9, 14) | 4.1, 4.3 |
| Behind all three: a buffer fund | Hold donor capital against the guarantees, so that they add to lending | Guarantees use capital (20, 21) | 4.2 |

# The macroeconomic profile and its indicators {#sec-macro}

**The literature agrees that the transition is a large investment program and disagrees on the sign of its growth effect.** Pisani-Ferry calls decarbonization an adverse supply shock, much like the oil shocks of the 1970s, with extra investment of at least 2 percentage points of GDP by 2030 [@PisaniFerry2021]. His report for the French government adds a temporary productivity slowdown of a quarter of a point a year and a risk to public debt of 10 points of GDP by 2030 and 25 by 2040 [@PisaniFerryMahfouz2023]. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) finds that near-term policies lower world growth by 0.15 to 0.25 points a year and raise inflation by 0.1 to 0.4 points [@IMF2022WEO]. The IEA's net zero path, with joint analysis by the IMF, has growth 0.4 points a year higher and world GDP 4 percent higher in 2030 [@IEA2021]. Green investment has multipliers of 1.1 to 1.5, against 0.5 to 0.6 for fossil investment [@Batini2021]. Studies after the fact are also split: Europe's carbon taxes show no negative effect on GDP or jobs and no effect on inflation [@MetcalfStock2023; @KonradtWeder2023], while a tightening of carbon policy lowers activity and burdens poorer households most [@Kanzig2026]. The split has a pattern. A transition led by prices is a supply shock. One led by financed investment adds demand first and supply later, and its sign turns on the cost of capital. In developing countries the program is larger: \$2.3 trillion to \$2.5 trillion a year by 2030 outside China [@IHLEG2024], and 5 to 6 percent of GDP in the Egypt illustration.

**The fiscal effect comes through four channels, and only one of them is a subsidy.** Fuel subsidies fall as fuel use falls. Fuel taxes fall with them: in the United Kingdom, receipts worth 1.6 percent of GDP are lost by 2050, three-quarters of them fuel duty, and net zero adds 21 percent of GDP to public debt; a levy on motoring that replaced the lost receipts would remove that increase [@OBR2021]. Public spending rises: a transition that relies mostly on spending could raise public debt by 45 to 50 percent of GDP by mid-century in a large emitter [@IMF2023FM]. And contingent liabilities rise. Guarantees to buyers of power join those already given to the fuel system, which in Egypt are 18 percent of GDP for the state oil company alone [@IMF2026Egypt56]. The gas fleet runs less while its fixed costs stay with the state utility. The fiscal question therefore moves from subsidies in the budget to guarantees on the balance sheet.

**The external accounts trace a J.** Much of the equipment is imported. Modules and inverters are about 35 percent of the installed cost of solar, turbines about three-quarters of the installed cost of wind, and China makes over 75 percent of the world's batteries [@IRENA2025]. This note takes half of capital spending as imported; no published split was found. That is no worse than the system it replaces. A gas plant also imports its turbines, and then imports fuel every year. In the Egypt illustration the external balance is worse by 1.7 percent of GDP at the start and better from 2032, or from 2034 once interest on the foreign finance is counted at the local rate (Appendix B). Long foreign finance must bridge those years.

**Monetary policy meets an energy system that is more sensitive to interest rates and less to fuel prices.** Higher interest rates raise the cost of renewable power far more than that of gas power [@Schnabel2023; @Monnin2015]. A tightening cycle therefore slows the transition unless finance is fixed-rate and long. In exchange, a clean system passes fewer fuel-price shocks into inflation and the trade balance.

**Time and capacity bind before money does.** Plants take 1 to 5 years and grids 5 to 15 [@IEA2023Grids]. Projects started while public investment is being scaled up are somewhat less likely to succeed [@Presbitero2016], and Africa added 11 of the 692 gigawatts of renewable capacity built in the world in 2025 [@IRENA2026Capacity]. Egypt's illustrative path adds 7.5 gigawatts of wind and solar a year. Its record is 1.5, though agreements signed for 2027–28 cover 17.4 [@IMF2026Egypt7]. The program is 6 percent of GDP in a country that invests 13 percent and saves 8 [@WDI2026]. Much of the engineering and the finance must therefore come from outside, as it already does: development banks lent four-fifths of the cost of Egypt's largest solar and storage project [@pvmag2026Obelisk]. The implication is to tender whole programs, under standard contracts, to consortia that bring both.

**A high discount rate hides the cost of waiting.** An investor who discounts at the local cost of capital sees little loss in waiting. A government should compare paths at one social discount rate, whatever the financing cost. At 6 percent, five years' delay in Egypt costs \$6 billion in present value if the program is financed at the local rate and \$32 billion if it is de-risked; for power and transport alone it costs \$23 billion and \$35 billion. Delay also burns 217 billion cubic meters more gas (Appendix B).

**Ten indicators track the move from a fuel bill to a capital bill, and each institution reads them differently.** @tbl-indicators gives them with Egypt's values. A finance ministry that reads them budgets for guarantees and for the accounts of state companies as it once did for subsidies, and it plans for fuel tax revenue to fall. A central bank watches the import bill for equipment and the terms of its finance alongside the fuel bill. A debt office manages the currency and maturity of the capital bill, and uses guaranteed borrowing where it lowers the price and lengthens the term, as Egypt's already reports that it does [@EgyptMoF2026Debt].

| Indicator | What it shows | Egypt |
|:---------------------|:------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Net gas imports | Exposure of the fuel bill | 21 billion cubic meters in 2025; output down from 70 (2021) to 42 |
| Gas import bill | Foreign currency spent on fuel | \$6.0 billion in the first half of 2026, up 73 percent |
| Energy subsidies in the budget | Distance of prices from cost | 0.8 percent of GDP in 2025/26; retail fuel at cost recovery since December 2025 |
| Interest payments | Room for a capital bill | About 73 percent of revenue |
| Guarantees to state oil company | Liabilities of the fuel system | 18 percent of GDP |
| Cost of capital | The price of a capital bill | Solar 9.7 percent in dollars (2020); Treasury bills 26 percent; IBRD loan 5.4–6.0 percent |
| Investment and saving | Capacity to finance at home | 13 and 8 percent of GDP (2024/25) |
| Renewable share of generation | Progress of the switch | 14 percent in 2025; target 42 percent by 2028 |
| Capacity against peak load | Risk of idle gas plant | 61 gigawatts against 40 |
| Record yearly wind and solar build | Capacity to build | 1.5 gigawatts (2025) |

Sources: @Enterprise2026Gas; @Enterprise2026Cost; @IMF2026Egypt7; @IMF2026Egypt56; @IRENA2023Finance; @Enterprise2026CBE; @IBRD2026Rates; @WDI2026; @Ember2026Data; @Enterprise2026Blackout; @Zawya2026Peak; @IRENA2026Capacity. {#tbl-indicators}

# Implications, and the case for a global green deal {#sec-deal}

**Six implications for macroeconomic policy follow from the facts taken together.** First, the cost of capital is an energy price: report it and target it as fuel prices are reported now. Second, judge carbon pricing by the whole effective price and by whether it is believed, and use it as one part of a package. Third, make commitments in contracts, because investors discount announcements. Fourth, move fiscal monitoring from subsidies toward guarantees, the accounts of state companies and the erosion of fuel taxes. Fifth, finance the J-curve with long foreign money, some of it in the supplier's currency. Sixth, count the cost of waiting at a social discount rate, and buy engineering and finance at program scale.

**A transition that pays may still come too late.** Each fact gives a reason. The return is only as good as the buyer's promise and the government's. It depends on grids and rules that other bodies control. The saving comes years after the spending. At a local cost of capital, the present value of waiting looks small. In the Egypt illustration the program's net savings to 2050 have a present value of −\$14 billion when it is financed at the local rate and +\$108 billion when it is de-risked, at the same 6 percent discount rate. The difference is finance, and no fact about technology closes it.

**Three of the facts cannot be answered by one country.** The fall in cost from deployment goes to every later buyer, so each country deploys too little (fact 12). Fuel that one country saves is partly burned by another (fact 16). And the standing of lenders who are paid first is finite and is held in common by the shareholders of the development banks (fact 20). These three are the case for a global green deal. Countries with strong balance sheets would supply guarantee capital and markets for clean goods. Countries with cheap sun and wind would supply reforms, contracts and deployment. The price of carbon would be credited across borders and not only charged at them. The next paper in this series sets out the terms of that exchange and what it would cost.

# Appendix B: First estimates for Egypt at two costs of capital {#sec-appb .appendix}

This appendix holds the modelling. It prices one program for Egypt at two costs of capital, by sector. The results are the author's illustrative calculations on public data and are not official estimates of any institution [@InvModelEgypt2026]. The recent reforms matter for reading them: Egypt brought retail fuel prices to cost recovery in December 2025, raised electricity tariffs in 2026, and has advanced its target of 42 percent renewable electricity from 2030 to 2028 [@IMF2026Egypt7].

**The program.** The program is a rapid transition path from the national investment model of the author's open tools, a stock-and-flow model of energy use, power capacity and vehicles [@StrettonWP63; @StrettonWP65]: fossil-free power by 2045, every new vehicle electric by 2040, and 80 percent of industrial fuel use abated by 2050. It reaches 38 percent renewable electricity in 2030, from 14 percent in 2025 [@Ember2026Data]. The comparison is a current-trends path. All values are in 2024 dollars. The model's clock starts in 2025; a program that starts in 2027 shifts each date by two years.

**The two rates, in real terms.** The local cost of capital is 8.2 percent. The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) reports 9.7 percent in nominal dollars for solar power in Egypt in 2020, from a survey of financiers, and a benchmark of 8.8 percent in real terms [@IRENA2023Finance]. The note takes the average of the two in nominal terms, 10.3 percent, and removes 2 percent dollar inflation. A high case uses 12.6 percent. The de-risked cost of capital is 3.9 percent: 6 percent in nominal dollars, the upper end of what an IBRD loan of the longest maturity costs today [@IBRD2026Rates], less the same inflation. The de-risked rate is a bound and not a forecast. It is what capital would cost if the whole program were financed at the rate at which the Bank lends to a government. A payment guarantee alone takes about 1.4 points off the local rate in the stylized case of paper 3.1 [@CFPB31].

**Net cost by sector.** The program needs \$266 billion of extra investment over 2026–35, 5.3 percent of GDP: \$118 billion in power, of which \$52 billion is grids and storage, \$88 billion in industry, \$25 billion in buildings, \$20 billion in transport and \$16 billion in other measures. By 2035 that capital costs \$25.6 billion a year at the local rate, against \$23.9 billion of fuel saved, and the program's net cost is \$3.0 billion, 0.5 percent of GDP. At the de-risked rate the capital costs \$17.1 billion and the program saves \$5.5 billion net, 0.9 percent of GDP (@tbl-sector, @fig-sector). Of the \$8.5 billion between the two capital charges, \$4.1 billion is in power, grids and storage, which is the part the three products of @sec-finance can reach. De-risking power alone turns the net cost of \$3.0 billion into a net saving of \$1.1 billion. A payment guarantee alone, on power alone, lowers the net cost to \$1.6 billion.

![Net cost by sector in 2035 at the local and the de-risked cost of capital, US\$ billion a year. Source: author's calculations [@InvModelEgypt2026].](2.Source/figures/fig2-net-cost-by-sector.png){#fig-sector width=88%}

**What the sectors show.** Power with its grids and storage pays for itself at any real cost of capital below about 15 percent. Solar costs \$34 per megawatt-hour at the local rate and \$24 de-risked, and wind \$40 and \$29, against \$90 for the fuel alone in a gas plant that burns imported gas. Transport pays from the early 2030s. Buildings break even just below 6 percent. Industry, on an assumed \$150 of capital for each gigajoule a year of fuel abated, breaks even only below 3 percent. The cost per tonne of carbon dioxide cut in 2035 is −\$82 in power and −\$134 in transport at the local rate, and +\$81 in buildings and +\$149 in industry; de-risked, the four are −\$125, −\$191, −\$54 and +\$34. For clean power with its grids and storage, de-risking is worth \$19 to \$20 per megawatt-hour, which is what a carbon price of \$43 to \$46 a tonne on the displaced gas would be worth. The levels are fragile: industry and buildings each rest on one assumed unit cost, and the results that carry weight are those for power and transport.

**A check against contracts and other estimates.** Egypt's recent contracts are at 2.4 to 2.5 US cents a kilowatt-hour for wind and solar, with sovereign guarantees and development-bank debt [@Zawya2026RedSea; @ACWA2024KomOmbo; @pvmag2026Obelisk]. That equals the model's de-risked cost. The leading projects are already de-risked by the government's own guarantee, so the gap in the model applies to the roughly 70 gigawatts that the path adds by 2035 beyond those already under agreement, which the government's balance sheet may not be able to carry. The World Bank's country climate report puts the extra investment in generation and storage for a net zero power path at \$96 billion over 2030–50 [@WorldBank2022CCDR]; the program here spends \$66 billion extra on generation in 2026–35 alone, because it moves earlier and faster. Egypt's own climate pledge costs its mitigation measures at \$196 billion to 2030 [@Egypt2023NDC].

**Who pays.** The model splits investment by where repayment comes from; the shares are judgments applied to country data [@StrettonWP65]. With tariffs and subsidies as in the 2024 data, the direct budget need in 2030 is 2.2 percent of GDP, half of it in power. De-risking alone lowers it to 2.0 percent. Cost-recovery tariffs, with fuel subsidies gone, lower it to 0.9 percent, and the need in power falls from \$5.3 billion to \$0.5 billion. Tariffs therefore matter more to the budget than the cost of capital, and the reforms of 2025–26 have already moved Egypt part of the way from the first case toward the third.

**Time path and external accounts.** Extra investment runs at 4 to 6 percent of GDP a year from the start; fuel savings reach 2.0 percent of GDP in 2030 and 4.0 percent in 2035 (@fig-path). With half of capital spending imported, the equipment bill exceeds the fuel saved until 2032. If the equipment is financed abroad and fuel savings repay the debt, the program's net foreign debt peaks at 7 to 8 percent of GDP in 2031–32 and is repaid by 2038–39. Counting interest, the effect on the external balance turns positive in 2032 at the de-risked rate and in 2034 at the local rate. By 2035 the imported equipment bought since the start comes to \$133 billion; interest on all of it would be \$5 billion to \$11 billion a year at the two rates, against fuel savings of \$24 billion. The fuel saved is gas that Egypt would otherwise import: 7 billion cubic meters in power stations in 2030 and 19 billion in 2035, against imports of 22 billion in 2025 [@Enterprise2026Gas].

![The time path of the program, percent of GDP. Left: extra investment, the half of capital spending taken as imported, and fuel saved. Right: fuel saved less imported equipment and less interest on the program's net foreign debt, at each cost of capital. Source: author's calculations [@InvModelEgypt2026].](2.Source/figures/fig3-time-path.png){#fig-path width=92%}

**Growth and debt.** Two macroeconomic models in the tools put GDP in 2030 above its level without the program by 0.9 percent and by 5.6 percent. Public debt in 2030 is 93 to 94 percent of GDP, against 91 percent without the program in the first model. They agree on the sign. They differ on whether private investment and energy savings are counted, and their calibrations are illustrative.

**The cost of waiting.** The test is to slip every milestone by five years and to compare present values to 2050 at one discount rate, 6 percent, whatever the financing cost. Financed at the local rate, the program's net savings on time have a present value of −\$14 billion, and waiting costs a further \$6 billion: \$23 billion lost in power and transport, less \$16 billion saved by postponing the sectors that do not pay. Financed at the de-risked rate, the program is worth +\$108 billion and waiting costs \$32 billion, of which \$35 billion is in power and transport. Either way Egypt burns 217 billion cubic meters more gas in power stations by 2050, pays \$206 billion more for fuel, undiscounted, and emits about 970 million tonnes more. Falling equipment costs do not reverse the result. The model lowers the cost of solar by 3 percent a year, and one year's additions of wind and solar left unbuilt burn \$1.8 billion of gas in that year.

**Scale.** The path adds 7.5 gigawatts of wind and solar a year. Egypt had 6.3 gigawatts at the end of 2025, and the most it has added in a year is 1.5 gigawatts [@IRENA2026Capacity]. Program investment in 2030 is 6.2 percent of GDP, in an economy that invested 13 percent of GDP in 2024/25 and saved 8 percent [@WDI2026].

**Method.** The model projects end-use energy at constant prices, builds the capital each path needs and values fuel at its cost to the economy. Net cost for each sector is the extra capital in service times a capital recovery factor over the asset's life (25 years for generation, buildings and industry, 40 for grids, 12 for vehicles), plus the change in running cost, less fuel saved. Unit costs are: solar \$760 per kilowatt and wind \$1,160 in 2024, falling 3 and 1.5 percent a year (world averages in 2024 were \$691 and \$1,041 [@IRENA2025]; Egyptian solar projects have cost \$536 to \$815 [@pvmag2026Obelisk; @ACWA2024KomOmbo]); batteries \$250 per kilowatt-hour, falling 3 percent a year; grids at \$0.60 for each dollar of generation investment; buildings \$200 and industry \$150 for each gigajoule a year of fuel displaced, both assumptions. The script that makes every number here, and its output, are in the note's source folder.

**Three choices that differ from the tool's defaults.** Capital is priced at world prices; the tool scales it by the local price level, 41 percent for Egypt after the 2024 float. Neither path builds new gas plant, because Egypt has 61 gigawatts of capacity against a peak load of 40 [@Enterprise2026Blackout; @Zawya2026Peak]. And gas for power and industry is valued at an import price of \$12 per million British thermal units, because Egypt has been a net importer since 2024: its imports cost about \$13 in the first half of 2026 (\$6.0 billion for 13.1 billion cubic meters [@Enterprise2026Cost; @Enterprise2026Gas]), against a supply cost of \$8.8 in the IMF's 2024 dataset [@Black2023]. @tbl-sens shows what each choice does.

**Limits.** The power mix follows target dates and does not respond to the cost of capital. Unit costs in buildings and industry are assumptions, and those sectors have no spending on the current-trends path, so their increments are upper bounds. The model has no hourly dispatch, so storage and grid needs are rules of thumb. The fuel values and tariff data are for 2024 and do not include the reforms of 2025–26. Three checks should come before the estimates are used: Egyptian plant data for industry and buildings, an hourly model of the power system, and a reconciliation with the budget and the accounts of the state energy companies. The inputs are public data. No internal or proprietary material of any institution is used.
